```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("R/setup.R")
r <- load_results()
m <- r$metrics[3,]
f <- r$group_metrics[1,]
male <- r$group_metrics[2,]
```

## The research question

We evaluate an enrolment-time warning using age at enrolment, admission grade and course. We then ask whether the same rule has different false-warning and missed-dropout rates across recorded-gender groups.

The historical records come from one Portuguese institution, not the University of Edinburgh. Recorded Dropout includes changes of course or institution. It is not a direct measure of leaving higher education altogether or of needing assistance.

## Outcomes and the analysis population

```{r outcome-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(r$outcomes, col.names=c("Recorded outcome","Records","Proportion"), digits=3)
```

The primary binary outcome is Dropout=1 and Graduate or Enrolled=0. Zero means no recorded Dropout at the normal course endpoint; it does not mean graduated or never dropping out later. The usual endpoint is three years, with four years for Nursing.

We retain all three labels and separately report a resolved-outcome sensitivity analysis excluding Enrolled. That check changes the population and question; it does not replace the primary result because of a more favourable score.

## Inputs and prediction time

Our primary inputs are age, admission grade and course. Numerical course codes represent categories, so we use a factor.

The twelve semester-end fields are unavailable at enrolment and are excluded. Financial statuses have uncertain individual recording times and are excluded conservatively. Macroeconomic fields may identify cohort differences indirectly, but no corresponding enrolment-year field is available; they are omitted from this small model.

In the training data, course determines attendance regime. We retain course without the redundant attendance term, before validation or test evaluation. The diagnostic is saved in `results/training-course-attendance.csv`.

The field audit is in `results/variable-timing-audit.csv`. No blank cells does not mean there are no unknown category codes or prior source-data exclusions.

## The probability model

The model is a fitted probability rule. A threshold converts each estimated probability into a warning decision.

```{r model-example, eval=FALSE}
fit <- glm(dropout ~ age10 + admission10 + course,
           data=training, family=binomial())
```

`glm` fits a generalised linear model; `binomial` specifies the binary logistic model. Dividing age and admission grade by ten changes their units; it is not standardisation estimated from test data. Course is categorical. Age and grade are linear on the log-odds scale, with additive course effects and no interactions. These are simplifying assumptions.

Logistic regression is supplementary to the supplied material. We explain it with the official R documentation rather than claiming it appeared in an uploaded modelling lecture.

## Training, validation and test records

```{r partitions, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Partition=c("Training","Validation","Test"),
  Records=c(r$configuration$training_n,r$configuration$validation_n,r$configuration$test_n),
  Purpose=c("Fit coefficients","Choose threshold","Evaluate the frozen rule")))
```

The random split is stratified by original outcome and recorded gender. It is not a national probability sample. Exact full-record profiles stay together within one partition. No cohort field is available for a chronological future-cohort test.

Test outcomes do not choose the main model, inputs or threshold. The validation records are not subsequently added into a refitted model.

## The threshold and illustrative sensitivity target

The warning threshold is `r num(r$threshold,2)`. On a pre-specified grid from 0.05 to 0.80, we choose the validation threshold with highest specificity among those attaining at least 70% sensitivity. The target is an illustrative analytical choice, not an agreed university policy or an established operational optimum.

A lower threshold generally produces more warnings. It can find more actual recorded dropouts while also warning more students without that label. This trade-off requires explicit interpretation.

## Reading the test results

```{r test-results, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(r$metrics, digits=3)
```

For the selected rule:

- It identifies 187 of 285 actual dropout records and misses 98: sensitivity is `r pct(m$Sensitivity)`.
- It warns 222 of 604 records without Dropout: the false-positive rate is `r pct(m$FPR)`.
- Of 409 warnings, 187 match a Dropout record: precision is `r pct(m$PPV)`.
- It warns `r pct(m$WarningRate)` of all test records, which matters for support capacity.

A false warning is an error relative to the administrative label. It does not establish that the student needs no support. The label does not reveal reasons for transfer or individual support needs.

## Three fairness criteria and their denominators

```{r fairness-rates, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Criterion=c("Independence","Separation","Separation","Sufficiency","Sufficiency"),
  Rate=c("Warning rate","False-positive rate","False-negative rate","Precision / PPV","Dropout among unwarned / FOR"),
  Female=pct(c(f$WarningRate,f$FPR,f$FNR,f$PPV,f$FOR)),
  Male=pct(c(male$WarningRate,male$FPR,male$FNR,male$PPV,male$FOR))))
```

The female false-negative rate is 64/144 and the male rate is 34/141. Comparing 64 with 34 alone ignores the conditional denominators. Full group sizes are 575 and 314, but only actual dropout records belong in the false-negative-rate denominators.

False-positive rates instead condition on records without Dropout. Male records have the higher false-warning rate, while female records have the higher missed-dropout rate. The error patterns therefore differ in more than one direction.

Binary Sufficiency requires both prediction strata. Precision alone omits outcomes among unwarned students. NPV is the non-dropout proportion among unwarned records; FOR=1-NPV is their recorded-dropout proportion.

Base dropout rates also differ: `r pct(f$BaseRate)` for female records and `r pct(male$BaseRate)` for male records. Gaps require investigation; they do not establish that gender causes dropout or that the model is discriminatory.

## Bootstrap intervals and calibration

The course bootstrap idea is to sample with replacement, recalculate statistics, repeat, and use the middle 95% of the distribution. Here we resample test records within recorded-gender groups, holding the model and threshold fixed, for `r num(r$bootstrap_reps)` repetitions.

```{r bootstrap-example, eval=FALSE}
sample_rows <- sample.int(nrow(group_data), replace=TRUE)
bootstrap_group <- group_data[sample_rows, ]
# After repeated group-rate calculations, take percentile limits:
quantile(gaps, c(0.025,0.975))
```

The female-minus-male false-negative-rate gap is about 20.3 percentage points, with a conditional interval of about 9.5 to 30.7 points. It excludes uncertainty from refitting, threshold selection, cohort clustering and transport to another institution. Separate pointwise 95% intervals do not provide a simultaneous 95% fairness guarantee.

Calibration concerns estimated probabilities: do records given about 30% probability have about 30% recorded dropout? Probability bins provide a descriptive check. They neither establish exact calibration nor replace binary Sufficiency at the warning threshold.

## Explaining our choices

We organise the explanation around the question, the choice and its implication. Enrolment-time prediction excludes later marks. The administrative label limits what dropout means. Training-only diagnostics avoid redundant inputs. Error trade-offs motivate reporting several metrics. Omitting gender does not remove the need for a group audit.

Our course/supplementary learning account and actual assistance are described in `docs/learning-process.md`.

## Reading and reproducing the R code

Open `student-dropout-final.Rproj`. `R/analysis.R` imports and defines records, audits variable timing, creates partitions and training summaries, fits and validates the model, evaluates test predictions, constructs bootstrap intervals, and saves the sensitivity checks and figures.

`presentation.Rmd` reads the saved results rather than manually copying numerical answers. `verify_project.R` independently checks raw-row identities, partitions, predictions, threshold selection and metric denominators.

The supplied material supports data import, factors, wrangling, joins, plotting, bootstrap ideas and the fairness criteria. Logistic regression, held-out evaluation, AUC/Brier and implementation helpers are explained as further learning. See `docs/course-map.md`.

## Remaining work and limits

The analysis, presentation and supporting documents do not replace topic-feasibility confirmation, actual group review, rehearsal, check-ins, accepted collaboration invitations, the separate report, peer evaluation or formal submission. We have not established that the warning reduces dropout or transfers reliably to Edinburgh.
